Chess Olympiad dataset: descriptive statistics¶

General overview of the Olympiad database (2010–2026, Open and Women's sections): who played, how strong they were, how games ended, how long they lasted, and what clock data exists.

Sources: The Week in Chess (all games, teams, boards, ratings, results) and Lichess broadcasts (clock readings and engine evaluations, 2018 onwards). 2020 and 2021 are excluded because those Olympiads were online rapid events.

Definitions used throughout

  • Played game: a game with a 1-0, ½-½ or 0-1 result and recorded moves. Games with no moves are left out, and so are decisive games of fewer than 5 moves, which are almost certainly forfeits.
  • Rated game: a played game where both players have a rating in the source file.
  • Team average rating: the mean rating of a team's players over the games they played in that Olympiad, so a player with more games counts more. Unrated players are left out of the mean.

To rerun: start the PostgreSQL server, set DATABASE_URL if it differs from the default below, and choose Run All.

What this shows

  • The Olympiad has grown from 5,746 games in 2010 to 8,645 in 2026. Of all 56,436 games, 55,799 count as played under the definition above.
  • Both players have a rating in 79–94% of played Open games per Olympiad, and in 74–89% of Women's games.
  • Clock data starts in 2018, covering 75–78% of games that year and 94–99% from 2022.
  • Teams and players are counted only if they played at least one game under this definition, so these totals can be slightly below the official entry lists.

What this shows

  • The median Open rating fell from 2,416 in 2010 to 2,203 in 2026, and the Women's median from 2,122 to 1,905. The Women's section sits about 300 points lower throughout. These figures cover rated players only, so part of the fall may reflect more low-rated players having a FIDE rating.
  • The Women's lower quartile jumps from 1,560 in 2022 to 1,726 in 2024, which fits the 2024 rating compression.
  • Mean rating falls steadily from board 1 to board 4: 2,337 to 2,205 in the Open and 2,053 to 1,890 in the Women's section.
  • Grandmasters make up 27.8% of Open entries. In the Women's section, 2.4% hold the GM title and 41.4% have no title listed.

How even are the matches?¶

The Olympiad is a Swiss tournament: after the first round, teams meet others with similar scores. The rating gap should therefore shrink after early rounds.

The match-level figures use only matches with four games on four distinct boards between exactly two teams, because some matches in the source files are split or mislabelled.

What this shows

  • The strongest Open team averages 2,743–2,764 in every Olympiad, while the mean team fell from 2,382 to 2,181. The field has widened below a stable top.
  • The strongest Women's team ranges from 2,450 to 2,534, and the mean team fell from 2,092 to 1,911.
  • Swiss pairing narrows the matches quickly. The median team rating gap in the Open falls from 498 in round 1 to 113 in round 11, and in the Women's section from 526 to 132. Most of that happens in the first three rounds.
  • About 13% of matches finish 2–2, and 25.5% of Open and 21.9% of Women's matches finish 2½–1½. Whitewashes (4–0) make up 19.9% and 24.7%.
  • Ratings predict match results well but not perfectly. With a gap under 25 points, the stronger team wins 40.4% of matches and the weaker team 34.1%. At 300 points or more, the stronger team wins 96.7%.

What this shows

  • The Open draw rate fell from 32.0% in 2010 to between 23% and 27% from 2014. The Women's rate stays between 18.6% and 23.8%.
  • Draws depend heavily on rating level. Below an average rating of 2000, about 17% of games are drawn in both sections. In the Open this reaches 60.6% at 2700–2800, and in the Women's section 58.7% at 2500–2600 (only 121 games).
  • Above 2000, Women's games at the same rating level are drawn more often than Open games: 39.4% against 23.7% at 2300–2400. This is a raw comparison with nothing controlled.
  • Draws also depend on how evenly matched the players are. The Open draw rate falls from 42.3% with a gap under 25 points to 6.8% at 400 or more, and the Women's rate from 33.0% to 6.2%.
  • White scores 53.5% in closely matched games. White's results run above the Elo formula when White is about equal or lower rated, and match it when White is much stronger.
  • Draw rates fall slightly from board 1 to board 4. They are very low in round 1 (6.8% Open, 3.8% Women's), when mismatches are largest, and settle at about 26–32% and 20–25% from round 3.

What this shows

  • The median game lasts 41–43 moves when decisive and 46–47 when drawn. Median length barely changes with rating level.
  • Draws jump sharply at move 30. There are 76 draws at exactly move 29 and 486 at move 30. In 2010, 24.5% of Open and 19.8% of Women's draws ended before move 30, compared with only 3–7% from 2012. This looks like a rule limiting early draw agreements that began after 2010, and should be confirmed in the Olympiad regulations. It matters when comparing draw rates over time, including the higher 2010 Open figure above.
  • 1.e4 is White's most common first move, at 46.3% in the Open and 55.3% in the Women's section. No single ECO code accounts for more than about 3% of games.

6. Clock and engine data¶

Clock readings exist only where Lichess broadcast data could be matched, so from 2018 onwards. The data records the time left after each move, not true timestamps. Thinking time and game duration are calculated from those readings.

Open 8 100 159 129 60 40 75 41 29 22 21

What this shows

  • Engine evaluations cover about half of moves in 2018, 71–87% in 2022, and at least 96% in 2024 and 2026.
  • The median game lasts about 3.4 hours, and the middle half of games lasts about 2.9–4.1 hours. Time after the last move is not recorded, so true durations are slightly longer.
  • Players move quickly in the opening (a median of 7–8 seconds on move 1), then think longest around move 15 (159 seconds in the Open, 183 in the Women's section).
  • Median thinking time falls to about 40 seconds by move 40, rises to 65–75 seconds on move 41 once the time control passes, then declines to about 20 seconds by move 80.
  • The median player has only about 5–6 minutes left by move 39, so time pressure before the first time control is common.

7. Data limitations¶

Points to keep in mind when reading these figures:

Count
Item
Games with no recorded moves, excluded 400
Decisive games of 1 to 4 moves, treated as forfeits and excluded 237
Played games with at least one unrated or unlisted player 8,656 (15.5%)
Games with no usable board number 47
Matches without exactly 4 games, including split or mislabelled ones 103
Player records without a FIDE ID, so one person may appear under two spellings 267 of 6,038
Games with clock data before 2018 0
  • Team names vary across years. 2010 uses country codes (GER) and later years use full names, with some spelling changes. Each Olympiad is internally consistent, so per-Olympiad team statistics are unaffected, but teams should not be tracked across years by name until these are standardised.
  • Ratings are as listed in the game files. The FIDE rating compression of March 2024 affects comparisons below about 2000 across years.
  • The missing 30-minute bonus. About 21% of long games from 2022 onwards show no clock bonus after move 40, mostly on low tables, and the reason is not yet known. Time left after move 40 is therefore not shown here.
  • Clock reconstruction. A small number of long thinks around move 40 are understated in the current version of the pipeline. Arbiter stoppages and time spent after the last move are not recorded.
